title: The Secret of the Old House

image.note: Title over the boarded-up old house at the estate edge, vines across the door, a bright yellow notice nailed to the gate; warm dusk light, a dignified sense of hidden history

pages.text:
1. The Yellow Notice
2. A House Full of Children
3. What the Elders Knew
4. Behind the Locked Door
5. The Name in the Ledger
6. Standing Before the Board
7. The House That Was Saved

The Secret of the Old House is an original Tafiya Estate story. It celebrates curiosity, respect for the past, and the power of one determined child to protect what matters. Itohan solves her mystery not by breaking rules or taking risks, but by asking questions, listening to elders, and gathering proof, the quiet tools of every good detective.

A bright yellow notice had appeared overnight on the boarded-up house at the far edge of the estate. Itohan stopped her bicycle and read it twice. "To be demolished," it said, "to make way for a new clubhouse." The old house had stood empty for as long as she could remember, its windows blind with dust, its gate chained shut.

image.note: Itohan straddling her bicycle at the chained gate, reading a bright yellow demolition notice; the old boarded house looms behind, vine-covered; her face serious

pages.text: "Nobody even goes in there," said Emeka, braking beside her. But Itohan kept staring at the sagging roof and the vine that had climbed clear across the door. "It was here before the estate," she said. "Before all the new houses. Doesn't that make you wonder what it was?" Idara wondered too. Something about pulling it down felt wrong.

image.note: Three children on bicycles at the gate: Itohan gazing up, Emeka beside her, Idara frowning thoughtfully; the sagging roof and vine-covered door of the old house fill the background

pages.text: That evening Itohan sat with Nana, turning the pages of her oldest photograph album. The pictures were soft and faded, browned at the corners. Then she stopped short. There, in a cracked black-and-white photograph, stood the very same house, bright and whole. And crowded on its steps, grinning at the camera, were dozens of children in neat uniforms.

image.note: Itohan and Nana on the green chair with a large old album open on their laps; a faded black-and-white photograph visible on the page showing the old house full of uniformed children; warm lamplight

pages.text: "Nana, that's the old house by the gate," Itohan gasped. Nana leaned close, and her face went soft with memory. "So it is," she said quietly. "That was no ordinary house, child. Long ago, before this was ever an estate, that was our schoolroom. The first one for miles around." Itohan's heart began to thud.

image.note: Close two-shot: Nana's face gentle with memory, finger resting on the old photo; Itohan wide-eyed and astonished; the album between them, lamplight warm

pages.text: The next morning the three friends went from door to door, asking the oldest residents what they remembered. Baba Sule, who had lived on the land longest of all, set down his tea and smiled. "That house?" he said. "That is where I learned to read. We all did. Every leader this town ever raised sat on those steps."

image.note: Baba Sule, an elderly man, seated on his veranda with a cup of tea, smiling warmly as he speaks; Itohan, Emeka and Idara sitting forward, listening intently; a modern estate home behind

pages.text: "There was a teacher," Baba Sule went on, his eyes far away. "The finest anyone here had known. Strict, but kind underneath. She turned market children into doctors and judges." He tapped the table. "Her name is written down, in the old school ledger. If that book still exists, it is inside that house." Itohan and Emeka exchanged a glance.

image.note: Baba Sule tapping the table with one finger, mid-memory; the three children leaning in, Itohan and Emeka catching each other's eye with dawning excitement

pages.text: They did not go in alone. That would have been foolish and unsafe, for the floors were rotten and the beams hung low. Instead Itohan wrote a careful letter to the estate manager, explaining everything. Impressed, he agreed to open the house himself, with Remigius from the gate to keep everyone safe. The chain came off with a groan.

image.note: At the old house door: the estate manager unlocking the heavy chain, Remigius steadying it, the three children waiting a careful step back; the low sagging beams visible inside the doorway

pages.text: Inside, dust hung in the air like smoke, and pale light fell through the broken shutters. Against the far wall stood a tall wooden cupboard, its doors locked fast. Remigius eased it open with a bar. On the shelf, wrapped in cloth against the damp, lay a thick, leather-bound book. Idara lifted it out with both hands, hardly daring to breathe.

image.note: Dusty interior lit by shafts through broken shutters; Remigius prising open a tall old cupboard; Idara reaching in for a cloth-wrapped leather book; on a high shelf a tiny ant sits cross-legged and unbothered amid the dust

pages.text: They carried the ledger out into the daylight and opened it on the bonnet of the manager's car. Page after page listed the names of children, year after year, in careful looping ink. And at the top of every page, signed with a firm hand, was the teacher's name: Miss Adunni Bello.

image.note: The heavy ledger open on a car bonnet in bright daylight; children and adults leaning over it; a page dense with old looping handwritten names, one name larger at the top

pages.text: "Miss Adunni," breathed Baba Sule, who had followed them out. "That was her. That was our teacher." The ledger held more than names. Tucked between the pages were letters from old pupils, now grown, thanking her from every corner of the world. The little house had shaped hundreds of lives. And now it was to be knocked down.

image.note: Baba Sule's face moved almost to tears, hand on the open ledger; old letters fanned across the page; the children solemn around him; the doomed house behind them

pages.text: Itohan knew what she had to do. With Emeka and Idara beside her, she asked to speak at the next estate board meeting. Her hands trembled, but her voice did not. She held up the faded photograph and the heavy ledger. "You cannot pull this house down," she said. "It is where our town first learned to read."

image.note: A modern estate meeting room, adults seated round a long table; small Itohan standing bravely at the head, holding up the old photograph in one hand and the ledger in the other; Emeka and Idara beside her

pages.text: The board members passed the ledger from hand to hand, murmuring. Some had grandparents in those very pages. The chairman took off his glasses and studied the photograph for a long, quiet moment. "A clubhouse we can build anywhere," he said at last. "But this, this we can only lose once." He set the notice aside.

image.note: The chairman, glasses in hand, gazing down at the faded photograph with a thoughtful, moved expression; the yellow demolition notice being laid face-down on the table; board members murmuring

pages.text: The yellow notice came down. In its place, workers arrived to mend the roof, clear the vines, and polish the old windows until they shone. Where dust had lain, shelves rose, filled with books for every child on the estate. Miss Adunni's ledger was set in a glass case by the door, open for all to see.

image.note: The old house transformed and bright: mended roof, clear windows, new bookshelves inside; the leather ledger displayed in a glass case by the door; workers finishing up; sunlight

pages.text: On opening day, the whole estate gathered on the steps where the schoolchildren had once stood. Baba Sule cut the ribbon with a shaking, happy hand. Above the door, a new sign read: THE ADUNNI BELLO HERITAGE LIBRARY. Itohan looked up at it and smiled. Some things, she thought, are far too precious to knock down.

image.note: A joyful crowd on the restored steps; elderly Baba Sule cutting a ribbon; a new sign above the door reading THE ADUNNI BELLO HERITAGE LIBRARY; Itohan gazing up, smiling; echo of the old photograph's composition
